questions.q: Who wrote the tragedy Romeo and Juliet?
questions.x: The play was probably written in the mid-1590s and is based on an earlier Italian tale. It is set in Verona.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel Pride and Prejudice?
questions.x: Published in 1813, it was first issued anonymously, credited only to 'the Author of Sense and Sensibility'.

questions.q: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
questions.x: Doyle was a physician. He based Holmes partly on Joseph Bell, a doctor known for his sharp powers of deduction.

questions.q: Who is the author of the Harry Potter series?
questions.x: Rowling reportedly conceived the idea for Harry while on a delayed train from Manchester to London in 1990.

questions.q: Who wrote The Hobbit?
questions.x: Published in 1937, it began as a story Tolkien told his children. He reportedly scribbled its first line on an exam paper.

questions.q: In Moby-Dick, what is the name of the captain obsessed with the white whale?
questions.x: Captain Ahab commands the whaling ship Pequod. He lost a leg to the whale on an earlier voyage.

questions.q: Who wrote A Christmas Carol?
questions.x: Dickens wrote this ghost story in just a few weeks in 1843, and it was published that December.

questions.q: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, what does Alice follow down the hole?
questions.x: The rabbit pulls a pocket watch from his waistcoat and says he is late. Alice follows out of curiosity.

questions.q: Who wrote The Great Gatsby?
questions.x: The novel was published in 1925. It is set on Long Island during the Jazz Age.

questions.q: Who wrote To Kill a Mockingbird?
questions.x: It appeared in 1960 and won the 1961 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. Lee drew on her childhood in Alabama.

questions.q: Who wrote the dystopian novel 1984?
questions.x: Published in 1949, it introduced phrases like Big Brother and Newspeak into everyday language.

questions.q: In Animal Farm, what kind of animal is the leader Napoleon?
questions.x: Orwell's 1945 fable satirizes the Russian Revolution. Napoleon is a boar who seizes control of the farm.

questions.q: Who wrote The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe?
questions.x: Lewis and Tolkien were friends and belonged to the same Oxford writing group, the Inklings.

questions.q: Which Spanish author wrote Don Quixote?
questions.x: Part one appeared in 1605 and part two in 1615. It is often called the first modern novel.

questions.q: Which Italian poet wrote The Divine Comedy?
questions.x: Dante completed it around 1320, and its three parts are Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek poet is traditionally credited with composing the Odyssey?
questions.x: Tradition says Homer was blind, but little is known about him. Scholars still debate whether one poet composed both the Iliad and the Odyssey.

questions.q: In Shakespeare's Hamlet, Hamlet is the prince of which country?
questions.x: The play is set at Elsinore castle. Shakespeare based the story on an old Danish legend about Amleth.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play features the moneylender Shylock?
questions.x: Shylock demands a pound of flesh as payment for an unpaid loan. The famous courtroom scene follows.

questions.q: Who wrote Frankenstein?
questions.x: Shelley began the story at age 18 during a rainy summer holiday in Switzerland, after a ghost-story challenge among friends.

questions.q: Which author wrote the vampire novel Dracula?
questions.x: Stoker's novel was published in 1897. Its Transylvanian count helped shape nearly every vampire story since.

questions.q: Who wrote Little Women?
questions.x: Alcott based the four March sisters on herself and her own sisters. The book came out in 1868.

questions.q: Which author wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer?
questions.x: Published in 1876, it draws on Twain's boyhood in Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River.

questions.q: In Oliver Twist, what does Oliver famously ask for more of?
questions.x: His request, 'Please, sir, I want some more,' shocks the workhouse master. It is one of the best-known scenes in Dickens.

questions.q: Who wrote The Wonderful Wizard of Oz?
questions.x: The book was published in 1900. Baum went on to write thirteen more Oz books.

questions.q: Who wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory?
questions.x: Dahl was a former fighter pilot. The book was published in 1964 and has been filmed twice.

questions.q: Which children's author wrote The Cat in the Hat?
questions.x: Seuss wrote it in 1957 using only a limited list of simple words, as a livelier alternative to dull school readers.

questions.q: Who wrote Winnie-the-Pooh?
questions.x: Milne named the bear after his son's teddy, and a real Canadian bear named Winnipeg also inspired the name.

questions.q: Which Scottish author created Peter Pan?
questions.x: Peter Pan first appeared in a 1904 play. Barrie left the rights to Great Ormond Street Hospital in London.

questions.q: How many dwarfs live with Snow White in the classic fairy tale?
questions.x: The Brothers Grimm gave the dwarfs no names. Names such as Doc and Grumpy came from the 1937 Disney film.

questions.q: What does Cinderella lose as she flees the ball in the classic tale?
questions.x: The glass slipper comes from Charles Perrault's 1697 version. In the Grimm version, the slipper is gold.

questions.q: Which Danish author wrote The Ugly Duckling and The Emperor's New Clothes?
questions.x: Andersen published his first fairy tales in 1835. Many of his stories, including The Little Mermaid, were original creations.

questions.q: Which Greek hero spends ten years trying to get home after the Trojan War?
questions.x: His long voyage is the subject of Homer's Odyssey. He is also known by his Roman name, Ulysses.

questions.q: In Greek mythology, who is the king of the gods?
questions.x: Zeus rules from Mount Olympus and wields the thunderbolt. His Roman counterpart is Jupiter.

questions.q: Which legendary British king ruled from Camelot with his Knights of the Round Table?
questions.x: The round table was said to remove any rank among the knights. Arthur's sword Excalibur is also part of the legend.

questions.q: Who wrote The Catcher in the Rye?
questions.x: Published in 1951, it is narrated by the restless teenager Holden Caulfield. Salinger later withdrew from public life.

questions.q: Who wrote the novella Of Mice and Men?
questions.x: Steinbeck took the title from a poem by Robert Burns. The story follows two migrant workers in California.

questions.q: Which French author wrote Les Miserables?
questions.x: Hugo finished the huge novel in exile in 1862. It follows the ex-convict Jean Valjean.

questions.q: Who wrote The Three Musketeers?
questions.x: Dumas serialized it in 1844. Fittingly, the hero d'Artagnan is not one of the three musketeers at first.

questions.q: Which Russian author wrote War and Peace?
questions.x: The novel is set during Napoleon's invasion of Russia. First published in installments in the 1860s, it runs well over a thousand pages.

questions.q: Who wrote Crime and Punishment?
questions.x: Published in 1866, it follows a poor student in St. Petersburg who commits a murder and wrestles with his guilt.

questions.q: Which French author wrote Around the World in Eighty Days?
questions.x: Verne's 1872 adventure follows Phileas Fogg on a wager. Verne is often called a father of science fiction.

questions.q: Who wrote the pirate adventure Treasure Island?
questions.x: Stevenson began the story by drawing a map of an island for his stepson. It introduced the one-legged pirate Long John Silver.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel Jane Eyre?
questions.x: It was published in 1847 under the pen name Currer Bell. The tale was an immediate success.

questions.q: Who wrote Wuthering Heights?
questions.x: Her only novel appeared in 1847 under the pen name Ellis Bell. Emily died the following year.

questions.q: In The Lord of the Rings, which hobbit carries the One Ring to Mount Doom?
questions.x: Frodo is Bilbo's nephew and heir. His loyal friend Sam accompanies him on the final stretch.

questions.q: In Harry Potter, what is the name of the school of witchcraft and wizardry Harry attends?
questions.x: Hogwarts is divided into four houses: Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw and Slytherin.

questions.q: Which Irish-born author wrote Gulliver's Travels?
questions.x: Published in 1726, this satire was a sharp attack on the politics and society of Swift's day, not simply a children's book.

questions.q: Which English author wrote Robinson Crusoe?
questions.x: Published in 1719, it is often considered one of the first English novels. It was inspired partly by a real castaway, Alexander Selkirk.

questions.q: Which British author wrote The Jungle Book?
questions.x: Kipling was born in India. The 1894 stories follow Mowgli, a boy raised by wolves, alongside Baloo and Bagheera.

questions.q: Who wrote The Little Prince?
questions.x: The author was also an aviator. His 1943 story, often translated into hundreds of languages, begins with a pilot stranded in the desert.

questions.q: Who wrote The Hunger Games?
questions.x: Published in 2008, the book is set in Panem. Collins said she was inspired in part by the Greek myth of Theseus and the Minotaur.

questions.q: In Macbeth, what supernatural trio prophesies that Macbeth will be king?
questions.x: The witches meet Macbeth and Banquo on a heath. Their predictions set the tragedy in motion.

questions.q: Which American writer penned the poem The Raven?
questions.x: Poe published it in 1845. Its refrain, 'Nevermore,' is spoken by the bird.

questions.q: Which English poet wrote 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud'?
questions.x: The poem, often called 'Daffodils', was inspired by a walk Wordsworth took with his sister Dorothy in the Lake District.

questions.q: What syllable pattern does a traditional haiku follow?
questions.x: The haiku is a Japanese form. English haiku often keep the 5-7-5 pattern, though in Japanese it counts sounds rather than syllables.

questions.q: How many lines does a sonnet traditionally have?
questions.x: Shakespeare wrote 154 sonnets. The Italian and English forms arrange the 14 lines differently.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek epic poem tells of the wrath of Achilles during the Trojan War?
questions.x: The poem opens with the word 'wrath.' It covers only a few weeks near the end of the ten-year war.

questions.q: Who wrote The Diary of a Young Girl, a famous account of hiding during World War II?
questions.x: Anne wrote the diary in hiding in Amsterdam. Her father Otto, the only survivor of the family, had it published in 1947.

questions.q: Which Brazilian author wrote The Alchemist?
questions.x: Published in 1988, the story of the shepherd Santiago became one of the most translated books by a living author.

questions.q: Which Dr. Seuss character tries to steal Christmas from the Whos of Whoville?
questions.x: How the Grinch Stole Christmas! appeared in 1957. The Grinch's heart is said to be two sizes too small.

questions.q: What is the name of the great lion who rules Narnia?
questions.x: Aslan is the Narnian creator and king. His name is the Turkish word for lion.

questions.q: In which Jane Austen novel do Elinor and Marianne Dashwood appear?
questions.x: Austen's first published novel appeared in 1811. Elinor represents sense and Marianne sensibility.

questions.q: What is the name of the sport Harry Potter plays on a broomstick?
questions.x: A Quidditch team has seven players, and catching the Golden Snitch ends the match and earns 150 points.

questions.q: In the fairy tale Rapunzel, what does she let down from her tower?
questions.x: The Brothers Grimm included the tale in their 1812 collection. The name Rapunzel refers to a leafy plant, rampion.

questions.q: In which Shakespeare play does the line 'To be, or not to be' appear?
questions.x: It begins Hamlet's famous soliloquy in Act 3. It is perhaps the most quoted line in English drama.

questions.q: Who wrote The Old Man and the Sea?
questions.x: The novella won the 1953 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. Hemingway received the Nobel Prize the following year.

questions.q: Who wrote Fahrenheit 451, a novel about a future where books are burned?
questions.x: The title refers to the temperature at which book paper is said to catch fire. Bradbury wrote it in the basement of a library.

questions.q: Which Canadian author wrote The Handmaid's Tale?
questions.x: The dystopian novel appeared in 1985 and is set in the Republic of Gilead. Atwood wrote much of it in West Berlin.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1932 dystopian novel Brave New World?
questions.x: The title comes from a line in Shakespeare's The Tempest. Huxley's novel imagines a society controlled by pleasure and conditioning.

questions.q: Who wrote the science fiction novel The War of the Worlds?
questions.x: Published in 1898, it describes a Martian invasion of England. A 1938 radio dramatization famously alarmed some listeners.

questions.q: What is the name of Captain Nemo's submarine in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea?
questions.x: Verne's 1870 novel imagined an electric-powered submarine. A league is a distance unit, so the title is a distance traveled, not a depth.

questions.q: Who wrote The Call of the Wild, a novel about a sled dog named Buck?
questions.x: Set during the Klondike Gold Rush, the 1903 novel drew on London's own time in Canada's Yukon.

questions.q: Which Mark Twain character travels down the Mississippi on a raft with the runaway Jim?
questions.x: Huckleberry Finn was published in 1884 and is told in Huck's own dialect, a bold choice for its time.

questions.q: Who is Sherlock Holmes's loyal friend and chronicler?
questions.x: Watson narrates most of the Holmes stories. He is an army doctor wounded in Afghanistan.

questions.q: Who is the villainous pirate captain in Peter Pan?
questions.x: Hook lost his hand to Peter, who fed it to a crocodile. The croc enjoyed the taste and now follows Hook everywhere.

questions.q: Which Canadian author wrote Anne of Green Gables?
questions.x: Published in 1908, it is set on Prince Edward Island. Anne is an orphan mistakenly sent to an older brother and sister.

questions.q: Who wrote the horse story Black Beauty?
questions.x: Sewell wrote it in 1877 from her sickbed, as a plea for kinder treatment of horses. She died a few months after it was published.

questions.q: Who wrote The Secret Garden?
questions.x: Published in 1911, it follows Mary Lennox, a lonely orphan who finds a hidden walled garden in Yorkshire.

questions.q: Which author and illustrator created Where the Wild Things Are?
questions.x: The 1963 picture book follows a boy named Max. It won the Caldecott Medal in 1964.

questions.q: Who wrote The Very Hungry Caterpillar?
questions.x: The 1969 book has holes punched through its pages to show where the caterpillar has eaten.

questions.q: In Roald Dahl's story, what does BFG stand for?
questions.x: Dahl published The BFG in 1982. The giant blows dreams into children's bedrooms through a trumpet.

questions.q: Who wrote the picture book The Giving Tree?
questions.x: Published in 1964, it tells of a tree that gives everything it has to a boy. Silverstein also wrote Where the Sidewalk Ends.

questions.q: Which English poet wrote the epic Paradise Lost?
questions.x: Milton was blind when he dictated the poem, which was first published in 1667. It retells the story of Adam and Eve.

questions.q: Which medieval English author wrote The Canterbury Tales?
questions.x: Chaucer wrote it in the late 1300s in Middle English. It has pilgrims telling stories on the road to Canterbury.

questions.q: In the Old English epic Beowulf, which monster does the hero fight first?
questions.x: Grendel attacks the hall of King Hrothgar. Beowulf later fights Grendel's mother and a dragon.

questions.q: Who wrote The Picture of Dorian Gray?
questions.x: Published in 1890, it was Wilde's only novel. Its title character stays young while his portrait ages.

questions.q: Which crime writer wrote Murder on the Orient Express?
questions.x: Christie published it in 1934, and its detective is Hercule Poirot. She is among the best-selling novelists in history.

questions.q: Who wrote the thriller The Da Vinci Code?
questions.x: Brown's 2003 novel opens with a murder in the Louvre. It sparked a boom of conspiracy-themed thrillers.

questions.q: Who wrote the Civil War novel Gone with the Wind?
questions.x: Published in 1936, it won the Pulitzer Prize the next year. It was Mitchell's only novel published in her lifetime.

questions.q: Who wrote Lord of the Flies?
questions.x: Published in 1954, it follows a group of schoolboys stranded on an island. Golding received the Nobel Prize in 1983.

questions.q: Who wrote Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
questions.x: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of the Oxford mathematician Charles Dodgson. He first told the story on a boat trip in 1862.

questions.q: Who wrote and illustrated The Tale of Peter Rabbit?
questions.x: Potter first told the story in a letter to a sick child in 1893. She self-published it in 1901 before a publisher took it on.

questions.q: In Charlotte's Web, what kind of animal is Charlotte?
questions.x: Charlotte saves the pig Wilbur by weaving words into her web. E. B. White published the book in 1952.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel The Kite Runner?
questions.x: Published in 2003, it was Hosseini's debut. The story is set in Afghanistan and later in California.

questions.q: Who wrote the adventure novel Life of Pi?
questions.x: The 2001 novel won the Booker Prize in 2002. It tells of a boy stranded in a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger.

questions.q: In Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis, what does Gregor Samsa turn into?
questions.x: Kafka's 1915 novella opens with Gregor waking to find the change. Kafka insisted the insect never be drawn on the cover.

questions.q: In which Shakespeare play does the mischievous sprite Puck appear?
questions.x: Puck, also called Robin Goodfellow, serves the fairy king Oberon. His mistake with a love potion drives the plot.

questions.q: Which storyteller in One Thousand and One Nights tells tales to delay her execution?
questions.x: She keeps the king curious by stopping each night on a cliffhanger. After 1,001 nights he spares her.

questions.q: Which dragon guards the treasure of the Lonely Mountain in The Hobbit?
questions.x: Smaug is killed by Bard the Bowman, who spots a bare patch in the dragon's armor. The Lonely Mountain is also called Erebor.

questions.q: Which Wonderland character famously shouts 'Off with her head!'?
questions.x: The Queen of Hearts is rarely actually seen carrying out her executions. The Red Queen is a different character from the sequel.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1850 novel The Scarlet Letter?
questions.x: Set in Puritan Boston, it follows Hester Prynne, who must wear a scarlet 'A'. Hawthorne added a preface about finding the old manuscript in a customs house.

questions.q: Who wrote the anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom's Cabin?
questions.x: Published in 1852, it sold hundreds of thousands of copies within a few years and stirred anti-slavery feeling in the North.

questions.q: What is the name of Don Quixote's loyal squire?
questions.x: Sancho is a simple farmer who joins Don Quixote hoping to be rewarded with the governorship of an island.

questions.q: Who wrote The Adventures of Pinocchio?
questions.x: Collodi serialized the tale in an Italian children's magazine from 1881. It has been translated into over 200 languages.

questions.q: Which Welsh poet wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
questions.x: Thomas wrote the poem for his dying father in 1951. He is also known for the radio play Under Milk Wood.

questions.q: Who wrote the Russian novel The Master and Margarita?
questions.x: Bulgakov wrote it in secret in the 1930s. It was not published until the 1960s, long after his death, and features a devil visiting Moscow.

questions.q: Which Colombian author wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude?
questions.x: Published in 1967, the novel tells of the Buendia family in the town of Macondo. Garcia Marquez won the Nobel Prize in 1982.

questions.q: Which Nigerian author wrote Things Fall Apart?
questions.x: Published in 1958, it is among the most widely read African novels. Its title comes from a poem by W. B. Yeats.

questions.q: In Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris, what is the hunchbacked bell-ringer called?
questions.x: Hugo's 1831 novel helped revive interest in the neglected Notre-Dame cathedral and spurred its restoration.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play features the magician Prospero?
questions.x: Prospero is the exiled Duke of Milan who lives on an island with his daughter Miranda. The play is thought to be among Shakespeare's last.

questions.q: Who is the scheming villain who manipulates Othello?
questions.x: Iago plants the false idea that Othello's wife Desdemona is unfaithful. He is one of Shakespeare's most notorious villains.

questions.q: In King Lear, which daughter refuses to flatter her father with grand speeches?
questions.x: Cordelia says she loves Lear as a daughter should. He banishes her, a decision that leads to disaster.

questions.q: In which year did William Shakespeare die?
questions.x: Tradition says he died on April 23, 1616, which was also his birthday. Cervantes died the same year.

questions.q: The subtitle of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein refers to which figure from Greek myth?
questions.x: The full title is Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans.

questions.q: What term describes a novel told through letters?
questions.x: Samuel Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa are classic examples. Dracula and Frankenstein also use letters and journals in their telling.

questions.q: What is a word that imitates the sound it describes, such as 'buzz' or 'sizzle', called?
questions.x: The term comes from Greek words meaning 'name-making'. Comics use onomatopoeia heavily for sound effects.

questions.q: How many syllables are in a standard line of iambic pentameter?
questions.x: Each line has five iambs, with an unstressed then stressed syllable. Shakespeare used it for much of his verse.

questions.q: Which Romantic poet wrote 'Ode on a Grecian Urn'?
questions.x: Keats wrote it in 1819. It ends with the line 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty.' He died of tuberculosis aged 25.

questions.q: In Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, what type of bird does the mariner shoot?
questions.x: The dead bird is hung around his neck as punishment. This is the origin of the phrase 'an albatross around one's neck.'

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'The Tyger', which begins 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright'?
questions.x: Blake published it in his 1794 collection Songs of Experience. He also engraved and painted his own books.

questions.q: Which American poet wrote 'The Road Not Taken'?
questions.x: Frost published it in 1916. It begins 'Two roads diverged in a yellow wood' and is often misread as a poem about bold individualism.

questions.q: In which US state did Emily Dickinson spend almost her entire life?
questions.x: She lived in Amherst, Massachusetts. Only a handful of her nearly 1,800 poems were published while she was alive.

questions.q: Which poet published the collection Leaves of Grass in 1855?
questions.x: Whitman revised and expanded the book throughout his life. He paid for the first edition himself.

questions.q: Which Edgar Allan Poe story from 1841 is often called the first modern detective story?
a: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
The Fall of the House of Usher
questions.x: It introduced the brilliant amateur detective C. Auguste Dupin, a model for Sherlock Holmes.

questions.q: Where is the novel Wuthering Heights set?
questions.x: The Bronte sisters grew up at Haworth in Yorkshire, on the edge of the wild moors that shaped the novel's atmosphere.

questions.q: What name did Thomas Hardy give to the region of southwest England in his novels?
questions.x: Hardy's Wessex is based on Dorset and neighboring counties. The name revived the old Anglo-Saxon kingdom.

questions.q: Under which pen name did Charlotte Bronte publish Jane Eyre?
questions.x: The three Bronte sisters all used male-sounding pseudonyms with the initials C, E and A.

questions.q: What was the real name of the novelist who wrote as George Eliot?
questions.x: Evans chose a male pen name so her fiction would be taken seriously. Her works include Middlemarch and Silas Marner.

questions.q: What was Mark Twain's real name?
questions.x: The name 'Mark Twain' comes from a riverboat call meaning two fathoms deep. Clemens was once a Mississippi riverboat pilot.

questions.q: What was George Orwell's real name?
questions.x: Blair took the pen name Orwell after the River Orwell in Suffolk. He was born in India in 1903.

questions.q: Who is the orphan hero of Dickens's novel Great Expectations?
questions.x: Pip rises from a village blacksmith's apprentice to a gentleman in London. The novel was serialized in 1860-61.

questions.q: What does Don Quixote famously attack, believing them to be giants?
questions.x: The scene gave English the phrase 'tilting at windmills', meaning to fight imaginary enemies.

questions.q: In The Lord of the Rings, in which land does Mount Doom lie?
questions.x: Mordor is the realm of the Dark Lord Sauron. The Ring can only be destroyed in the fires where it was forged.

questions.q: Who wrote the science fiction epic Dune?
questions.x: Published in 1965, it is set on the desert planet Arrakis and is often cited as the best-selling science fiction novel.

questions.q: Which author formulated the fictional Three Laws of Robotics?
questions.x: The first law says a robot may not harm a human. Asimov explored the laws in stories collected in I, Robot.

questions.q: In The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, what is the answer to life, the universe and everything?
questions.x: The supercomputer Deep Thought takes 7.5 million years to compute it. Then it points out that nobody knew what the question was.

questions.q: Who wrote A Wizard of Earthsea?
questions.x: Published in 1968, it follows the young wizard Ged. Le Guin's book helped establish modern fantasy for young readers.

questions.q: Who wrote the cyberpunk novel Neuromancer?
questions.x: Published in 1984, it won the Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards. It popularized the idea of cyberspace.

questions.q: Which Philip K. Dick novel inspired the film Blade Runner?
a: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
The Man in the High Castle
questions.x: The 1968 novel follows a bounty hunter chasing rogue androids. The 1982 film changed much of the plot.

questions.q: Which H. G. Wells novel features the Eloi and the Morlocks?
a: The First Men in the Moon
questions.x: Published in 1895, it describes two human descendants living in the year 802,701.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek storyteller is traditionally credited with fables like The Tortoise and the Hare?
questions.x: Aesop is said to have lived around 600 BC and possibly been a slave. Many fables credited to him were collected long after his time.

questions.q: What were the first names of the Brothers Grimm?
questions.x: They collected German folk tales and published them from 1812. They were also scholars of language and wrote a German dictionary.

questions.q: Which French author published Cinderella and Puss in Boots in a 1697 collection?
questions.x: His Tales of Mother Goose helped create the fairy-tale genre in literature. It included Sleeping Beauty and Little Red Riding Hood.

questions.q: In which city is the famous statue of Hans Christian Andersen's Little Mermaid?
questions.x: The bronze statue on the waterfront was unveiled in 1913. It is only about 1.25 meters tall.

questions.q: Which sailor of One Thousand and One Nights goes on seven fantastic voyages?
questions.x: Sinbad's tales feature giant birds and sea monsters. They were added to the collection by later translators and storytellers.

questions.q: In Greek myth, who flew too close to the sun on wings made of wax and feathers?
questions.x: His father Daedalus built the wings to escape Crete. Icarus ignored his warning and fell into the sea.

questions.q: Which Greek hero beheaded the Gorgon Medusa?
questions.x: Perseus used a polished shield as a mirror to avoid her stone-turning gaze. Pegasus sprang from her blood.

questions.q: Which monster lived in the Labyrinth on Crete in Greek myth?
questions.x: The Minotaur had a bull's head and a man's body. The hero Theseus killed it with help from Ariadne's thread.

questions.q: What is the name of Thor's hammer in Norse mythology?
questions.x: Mjolnir was made by dwarves. The Norse god of thunder used it against the giants.

questions.q: Which Norse god is known as a shape-shifting trickster?
questions.x: Loki fathered monsters such as the wolf Fenrir. In the myths he helps the gods at times and opposes them at others.

questions.q: Which Roman poet wrote the Aeneid?
questions.x: The epic tells of the Trojan hero Aeneas and the founding of Rome. Virgil died in 19 BC before finishing revisions.

questions.q: Which Roman poet wrote the Metamorphoses?
questions.x: Ovid's poem retells myths of transformation, from Daphne becoming a laurel tree to Narcissus becoming a flower.

questions.q: In which ancient region was the Epic of Gilgamesh composed?
questions.x: The poem was written on clay tablets in cuneiform. It is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian epic tells the story of Rama and his wife Sita?
questions.x: Traditionally credited to the sage Valmiki, it has been retold across South and Southeast Asia in many languages.

questions.q: Which Chinese classic novel features the Monkey King, Sun Wukong?
questions.x: The 16th-century novel follows a monk's pilgrimage to India to fetch sacred texts. It is one of China's Four Great Classical Novels.

questions.q: Which German writer wrote the drama Faust?
questions.x: Goethe worked on Faust for most of his adult life, finishing the second part in the year he died, 1832.

questions.q: Pushkin's Eugene Onegin is unusual because it is a novel written in what form?
questions.x: Pushkin called it a 'novel in verse' and wrote it in a special 14-line stanza now known as the Onegin stanza.

questions.q: In which year did Ernest Hemingway win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: The Swedish Academy cited his mastery of narrative art, shown in The Old Man and the Sea. He was in Cuba and did not travel to Stockholm.

questions.q: Who in 1907 became the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Kipling was 41 and remains the youngest-ever winner of the prize in literature.

questions.q: Which Indian poet became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1913?
questions.x: Tagore was honored for Gitanjali. He also wrote the lyrics of the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

questions.q: Which author of Beloved won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Morrison was the first African American woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. Beloved won the Pulitzer Prize in 1988.

questions.q: What term describes the repetition of the same initial consonant sound, as in 'Peter Piper picked a peck'?
questions.x: Alliteration is common in tongue twisters, poetry and advertising slogans. Old English poetry such as Beowulf relied on it.

questions.q: What term describes a story whose characters and events symbolize deeper meanings, as in Animal Farm?
questions.x: Pilgrim's Progress by John Bunyan is another famous allegory. Its characters have names like Christian and Mr. Worldly Wiseman.

questions.q: How many lines does a limerick have?
questions.x: Limericks follow an AABBA rhyme scheme and are usually humorous. Edward Lear popularized the form in the 1800s.

questions.q: In Edward Lear's poem, what color is the boat in which the Owl and the Pussy-cat go to sea?
questions.x: They sail with honey and plenty of money wrapped in a five-pound note, then marry on a hill where the bong-tree grows.

questions.q: Which Lewis Carroll poem begins 'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves'?
questions.x: It appears in Through the Looking-Glass. Carroll's invented words, like chortle and galumphing, have entered English.

questions.q: Which T. S. Eliot poetry collection inspired the musical Cats?
a: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats
questions.x: Eliot published it in 1939 and signed it with his nickname, Old Possum. Andrew Lloyd Webber set it to music in 1981.

questions.q: Which 1922 poem by T. S. Eliot begins 'April is the cruellest month'?
a: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
questions.x: Ezra Pound heavily edited the draft, cutting it down to a landmark of modernist poetry.

questions.q: Which Oscar Wilde play features the formidable Lady Bracknell?
questions.x: The 1895 comedy is subtitled 'A Trivial Comedy for Serious People.' Lady Bracknell famously exclaims 'A handbag?'

questions.q: Which George Bernard Shaw play inspired the musical My Fair Lady?
questions.x: Shaw's 1913 play follows a phonetics professor teaching a flower seller to speak like a lady. Its title comes from a Greek myth.

questions.q: Which Russian playwright wrote The Seagull and Uncle Vanya?
questions.x: Chekhov was also a medical doctor. His plays, including Three Sisters, are staples of world theater.

questions.q: Which Norwegian dramatist wrote A Doll's House?
questions.x: Premiered in 1879, the play caused controversy when its heroine Nora walked out on her family in the final scene.

questions.q: Which Arthur Miller play is set during the Salem witch trials?
questions.x: Written in 1953, it used the 1692 trials as an allegory for McCarthyism in the United States.

questions.q: Which Tennessee Williams play features the character Blanche DuBois?
a: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
questions.x: The 1947 play won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. Marlon Brando starred in the 1951 film adaptation.

questions.q: Which Irish writer wrote the play Waiting for Godot?
questions.x: Beckett first wrote it in French in the early 1950s. It features two men waiting for someone who never arrives.

questions.q: Which Dickens novel opens with 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'?
questions.x: The 1859 novel is set in London and Paris before and during the French Revolution.

questions.q: Which novel opens with the line 'Call me Ishmael.'?
questions.x: Melville's 1851 whaling novel sold poorly during his lifetime. Its opening is among the most famous in American literature.

questions.q: Which novel begins 'Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way'?
questions.x: Tolstoy's 1878 novel opens with this line. It follows a married woman whose affair challenges Russian high society.

questions.q: Which Beat Generation author wrote On the Road?
questions.x: Published in 1957, it was reportedly typed on a single long scroll of paper in just a few weeks.

questions.q: Which author wrote the World War II satire Catch-22?
questions.x: Published in 1961, the novel gave English the phrase 'catch-22' for a no-win situation with contradictory rules.

questions.q: Which horror writer wrote The Shining?
questions.x: King's 1977 novel is set in the isolated Overlook Hotel. Stanley Kubrick adapted it into a 1980 film.

questions.q: Which French author wrote The Stranger?
questions.x: Published in 1942, the novel opens with the narrator Meursault learning of his mother's death. Camus won the Nobel Prize in 1957.

questions.q: Which author wrote the 1981 novel Midnight's Children?
questions.x: It won the Booker Prize in 1981 and again earned the Booker of Bookers award in 1993. Its narrator was born at the moment of India's independence.

questions.q: In which city did Franz Kafka live most of his life?
questions.x: Kafka was born in Prague in 1883 and wrote in German. Most of his major works were published after his death.

questions.q: Which Hemingway novel, set in the Spanish Civil War, takes its title from a John Donne meditation?
questions.x: Donne's lines include 'never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.' Hemingway published the novel in 1940.

questions.q: What is the title of Lewis Carroll's 1871 sequel to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
questions.x: The sequel's world is based on a chess game. Carroll's original draft of the first book was titled Alice's Adventures Under Ground.

questions.q: What are the workers in Willy Wonka's chocolate factory called?
questions.x: In Dahl's first version of the book, the factory workers were African pygmies. He revised them into the orange-skinned Oompa-Loompas in later editions.

questions.q: What is the name of Bilbo Baggins's sword in The Hobbit?
questions.x: The elvish blade glows blue when orcs or goblins are near. Bilbo later gives it to his nephew Frodo.

questions.q: What is the name of Mr. Darcy's estate in Pride and Prejudice?
questions.x: Elizabeth Bennet's visit to Pemberley changes her opinion of Darcy. Netherfield is the house rented by Mr. Bingley.

questions.q: In Little Women, which March sister dreams of being a writer?
questions.x: Jo is based on Louisa May Alcott herself. Her real name is Josephine.

questions.q: What is the name of Phileas Fogg's French valet in Around the World in Eighty Days?
questions.x: Passepartout means 'goes everywhere' in French. He is Fogg's loyal companion on the whole wager.

questions.q: In The Count of Monte Cristo, in which prison is Edmond Dantes held?
questions.x: The Chateau d'If is a real island fortress off Marseille. Dumas's story made it a world-famous tourist site.

questions.q: What is Sherlock Holmes's fictional London address?
questions.x: When the stories were written, no 221 existed on Baker Street. A museum now stands at the address.

questions.q: What nationality is Agatha Christie's detective Hercule Poirot?
questions.x: Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer living in England. He debuted in 1920 in The Mysterious Affair at Styles.

questions.q: In Orwell's 1984, who is the leader whose face appears on posters saying 'is watching you'?
questions.x: Big Brother is the figurehead of the Party. The slogan on the posters says 'Big Brother is watching you.'

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Ozymandias'?
questions.x: Shelley wrote it in 1817 about a ruined statue of a once-great king in the desert. The poem reflects on the fading of power.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'The Charge of the Light Brigade'?
questions.x: Tennyson wrote it in 1854 shortly after reading a newspaper report of the doomed cavalry attack in the Crimean War.

questions.q: Who is the teenage narrator of The Catcher in the Rye?
questions.x: Holden recounts a few days in New York after being expelled from his prep school, Pencey.

questions.q: In The Hobbit, who loses the magic ring to Bilbo after a game of riddles in the dark?
questions.x: Gollum bets the ring against Bilbo in the riddle game. Bilbo wins by asking 'What have I got in my pocket?'

questions.q: Which Charles Dickens story features the miser Ebenezer Scrooge?
questions.x: Three ghosts visit Scrooge on Christmas Eve and change his heart.

questions.q: Which Japanese court lady wrote The Tale of Genji in the early 11th century?
questions.x: The Tale of Genji is often called the world's first novel. Sei Shonagon, her contemporary, wrote The Pillow Book.

questions.q: Which Persian poet composed the epic Shahnameh, the 'Book of Kings'?
questions.x: Ferdowsi spent around thirty years on the poem of about 50,000 couplets, finishing it around the year 1010.

questions.q: In Gulliver's Travels, what is the name of the flying island that Gulliver visits?
questions.x: Laputa floats above the land of Balnibarbi and is home to absent-minded scientists. Swift used it to mock the learned societies of his day.

questions.q: Which Argentine writer wrote the story collection Ficciones?
questions.x: Published in 1944, it includes The Garden of Forking Paths and The Library of Babel. Borges worked for years as a librarian and became blind later in life.

questions.q: Which Chilean poet won the 1971 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Neruda was also a diplomat. His works include Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair. Mistral, another Chilean, won in 1945.

questions.q: Which American novelist won the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Steinbeck's books include The Grapes of Wrath and East of Eden. The Swedish Academy praised his realism and sympathetic humor.

questions.q: Which French philosopher and writer declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Sartre said he always refused official honors. His works include the novel Nausea and the play No Exit.

questions.q: Which Hermann Hesse novel follows a young man on a spiritual search in ancient India?
questions.x: Published in 1922, it is set in the time of the Buddha. Hesse won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946.

questions.q: Which novel opens with the line 'Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again'?
questions.x: Daphne du Maurier published Rebecca in 1938. The unnamed narrator never learns the first name of the title character's husband's new wife in the story, and is simply called the second Mrs. de Winter.

questions.q: In Orwell's 1984, what time are the clocks striking in the novel's famous first line?
questions.x: The first sentence reads 'It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.' The odd detail signals that this world is not our own.

questions.q: In which fictional village does Agatha Christie's Miss Marple live?
questions.x: Miss Marple first appeared in the 1927 short story The Tuesday Night Club. She solves crimes by comparing them to village gossip.

questions.q: Who guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory in the Divine Comedy?
questions.x: Dante picked Virgil as the model of human reason. Beatrice takes over to lead him through Paradise.

questions.q: In The Canterbury Tales, at which inn do the pilgrims meet before setting out?
questions.x: The Tabard Inn stood in Southwark, south of the Thames in London. The pilgrims agree to a storytelling contest on the way to Canterbury.

questions.q: In what language was the epic Beowulf originally composed?
questions.x: The only surviving manuscript dates from around the year 1000. The poem is set in Scandinavia, though it was composed in England.

questions.q: In the 14th-century Arthurian poem about a green challenger, which knight accepts the beheading game?
questions.x: Gawain is King Arthur's nephew. The 14th-century poem survives in a single manuscript, possibly written by the anonymous Pearl Poet.

questions.q: Who wrote Le Morte d'Arthur, printed by William Caxton in 1485?
questions.x: Malory is thought to have written it while imprisoned. It remains the best-known English version of the Arthurian legends.

questions.q: Which Elizabethan poet wrote the allegorical epic The Faerie Queene?
questions.x: Spenser wrote it in honor of Queen Elizabeth I and published the first books in 1590. He invented the Spenserian stanza for it.

questions.q: Which Elizabethan playwright wrote Doctor Faustus?
questions.x: Marlowe was born in the same year as Shakespeare, 1564. He was killed in a tavern brawl in 1593 at the age of 29.

questions.q: Which playwright wrote the satirical comedy Volpone?
questions.x: Jonson first staged Volpone around 1606. Its title means 'sly fox' and it is set in Venice.

questions.q: Which poet wrote the line 'To err is human; to forgive, divine'?
questions.x: It appears in An Essay on Criticism (1711). The same poem gave us 'a little learning is a dangerous thing' and 'fools rush in where angels fear to tread.'

questions.q: Which writer published A Dictionary of the English Language in 1755?
questions.x: Johnson compiled it largely by himself in about nine years. It defined thousands of words with quotations from famous writers.

questions.q: Who wrote the comic novel Tom Jones?
questions.x: Fielding published The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling in 1749. He was also a magistrate and helped found London's Bow Street Runners.

questions.q: Which 18th-century novel by Laurence Sterne is famous for its digressions and a narrator who struggles to tell his own life story?
questions.x: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman appeared from 1759 to 1767. It includes a black page and a marbled page, a playful experiment in book design.

questions.q: Which Scottish author wrote the historical novel Ivanhoe?
questions.x: Published in 1819, Ivanhoe is set in 12th-century England and features Robin Hood, called Locksley. Scott helped popularize the historical novel.

questions.q: Who wrote Vanity Fair, which features the ambitious Becky Sharp?
questions.x: The novel was serialized in 1847-48 and carries the subtitle 'A Novel without a Hero.' Thackeray also drew its illustrations.

questions.q: In which George Eliot novel does the idealistic Dorothea Brooke appear?
questions.x: Middlemarch (1871-72) is set in a fictional English Midlands town. Virginia Woolf called it one of the few English novels written for grown-up people.

questions.q: Which Polish-born novelist wrote Heart of Darkness?
questions.x: Conrad was born Jozef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski. He learned English as an adult after years at sea and wrote the novella in 1899.

questions.q: Who wrote the ghost story The Turn of the Screw?
questions.x: James published it in 1898. Readers still debate whether the ghosts are real or only the governess's imagination.

questions.q: Which Edith Wharton novel won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction?
questions.x: Wharton was the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. The novel is set in the high society of 1870s New York.

questions.q: Which Mississippi author wrote The Sound and the Fury?
questions.x: Faulkner published it in 1929. It is told in four sections, the first narrated by a man with an intellectual disability. He won the Nobel Prize in 1949.

questions.q: Which Virginia Woolf novel follows a single day in the life of a London hostess preparing for a party?
questions.x: Published in 1925, the novel moves between the minds of several characters. It begins with the hostess saying she will buy the flowers herself.

questions.q: On what date is James Joyce's Ulysses set, now celebrated as Bloomsday?
questions.x: The date marks Joyce's first outing with his future wife, Nora Barnacle. The novel follows Leopold Bloom through a single day in Dublin.

questions.q: In Proust's In Search of Lost Time, what small cake triggers the narrator's memories?
questions.x: The narrator dips the cake in tea and is flooded with childhood memories. 'Proustian' now describes a memory triggered by taste or smell.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel Madame Bovary, published in 1857?
questions.x: Flaubert was prosecuted for offending public morals over the book but was acquitted. He was famously obsessed with finding le mot juste, the exact word.

questions.q: Which Russian author wrote the satirical novel Dead Souls?
questions.x: The 1842 novel follows a con man buying the names of dead serfs. Gogol also wrote the play The Government Inspector.

questions.q: Which Russian author won the 1958 Nobel Prize in Literature but was pressured to decline it?
questions.x: Pasternak's novel Doctor Zhivago was banned in the Soviet Union and first published in Italy in 1957. Soviet officials forced him to refuse the prize.

questions.q: Which Soviet author wrote One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich?
questions.x: The 1962 novella draws on the author's own years in a labor camp. Solzhenitsyn won the Nobel Prize in 1970.

questions.q: Which Swedish playwright wrote Miss Julie?
questions.x: Strindberg wrote the play in 1888. It takes place in a single room during one midsummer night and is a landmark of naturalist drama.

questions.q: Which Swedish author was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1909?
questions.x: Lagerlof also wrote The Wonderful Adventures of Nils, a children's geography reader. Undset, a Norwegian, won in 1928.

questions.q: Which Swedish author created Pippi Longstocking?
questions.x: The first Pippi book appeared in 1945. Lindgren invented the stories while sitting at the bedside of her sick daughter.

questions.q: Which Finnish author and artist created the Moomins?
questions.x: Jansson wrote in Swedish, which is Finland's second official language. The first Moomin book appeared in 1945.

questions.q: Which Italian scholar wrote the medieval murder mystery The Name of the Rose?
questions.x: Published in 1980, it is set in an abbey in 1327. Eco was a professor of semiotics at the University of Bologna.

questions.q: Which Italian author wrote the Decameron, in which ten young people tell tales while escaping the plague?
questions.x: The group flees plague-stricken Florence in 1348 and tells 100 tales over ten days. Chaucer borrowed from Boccaccio.

questions.q: Who was the woman celebrated in Petrarch's love sonnets?
questions.x: Petrarch said he first saw her in a church in Avignon in 1327. The Petrarchan sonnet form is named after him.

questions.q: Which French playwright wrote the comedy Tartuffe?
questions.x: Moliere's 1664 comedy about a religious hypocrite was banned for several years after powerful figures objected. He collapsed on stage in 1673 during a performance of The Imaginary Invalid.

questions.q: Which 1759 satire by Voltaire follows an optimistic young man and his tutor Pangloss?
questions.x: Pangloss insists that this is the best of all possible worlds despite the disasters that follow. Voltaire's tale mocks facile optimism.

questions.q: Who wrote the play Cyrano de Bergerac?
questions.x: First staged in 1897, the play features a poet with an enormous nose. The real Cyrano de Bergerac was a 17th-century writer and duelist.

questions.q: Which Egyptian novelist won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote the Cairo Trilogy?
questions.x: Mahfouz was the first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. His trilogy follows a Cairo family across three generations.

questions.q: Which Japanese author of Snow Country won the 1968 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Kawabata was the first Japanese writer to receive the prize. Kenzaburo Oe followed in 1994.

questions.q: Who wrote the Japanese satirical novel I Am a Cat, published in 1905?
questions.x: The novel is narrated by a cat who observes the foibles of his human owner's circle. Soseki also wrote Kokoro and Botchan.

questions.q: Who wrote the 18th-century Chinese novel Dream of the Red Chamber?
questions.x: Cao Xueqin did not live to finish it, and later editors added the last forty chapters. It is one of China's Four Great Classical Novels.

questions.q: Which Nigerian playwright became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986?
questions.x: Soyinka's works include the play Death and the King's Horseman. He was also imprisoned during the Nigerian civil war.

questions.q: Which Chilean author wrote the 1982 novel The House of the Spirits?
questions.x: Allende began the book as a letter to her dying grandfather while in exile in Venezuela. It follows the Trueba family across generations.

questions.q: Which author wrote the Arthurian fantasy The Once and Future King?
questions.x: White published it as a single volume in 1958. Its first part, The Sword in the Stone, was adapted by Disney.

questions.q: Which German author wrote The Neverending Story?
questions.x: Published in 1979, it follows a boy who reads a book that pulls him into the land of Fantastica. Ende also wrote Momo.

questions.q: Which was the first Chronicles of Narnia book to be published, in 1950?
a: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
questions.x: The Magician's Nephew comes first in the story's chronology but was published in 1955.

questions.q: What was the title of Dr. Seuss's first children's book, published in 1937?
a: And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street
questions.x: Rejected by many publishers, it finally came out in 1937. Seuss later said he was about to burn the manuscript when he ran into an old friend who worked in publishing.

questions.q: In which year was Frankenstein first published?
questions.x: The first edition appeared anonymously in 1818. Mary Shelley's name was first printed on the 1823 edition and she revised the text in 1831.

questions.q: In which year was Bram Stoker's Dracula published?
questions.x: Stoker based the title on Vlad the Impaler's name, Dracula. He also worked as the business manager of the Lyceum Theatre in London.

questions.q: Jane Eyre and Wuthering Heights were both published in which year?
questions.x: Charlotte's Jane Eyre came out in October and Emily's Wuthering Heights in December. Anne's Agnes Grey appeared with the latter.

questions.q: In which year was Pride and Prejudice first published?
questions.x: Austen sold the copyright for 110 pounds. It was her second published novel.

questions.q: In which year was Melville's Moby-Dick first published?
questions.x: Moby-Dick got mixed reviews and sold poorly. Its reputation grew in the 20th century, decades after Melville died in 1891.

questions.q: In which year was the first part of Don Quixote published?
questions.x: Cervantes published the second part in 1615. A spurious sequel by another writer had appeared in 1614 and prompted him to finish his own.

questions.q: In which 1920 play did the word 'robot' first appear?
questions.x: The Czech play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) by Karel Capek premiered in 1921. The word comes from the Czech robota, meaning forced labor.

questions.q: Which World War I poet wrote 'Dulce et Decorum Est'?
questions.x: Owen was killed in 1918, one week before the Armistice. Only a handful of his poems were published in his lifetime.

questions.q: Which Canadian doctor wrote the poem 'In Flanders Fields'?
questions.x: McCrae wrote it in 1915 after a friend's death. The poem helped make the red poppy a symbol of remembrance.

questions.q: Which poet laureate wrote the Arthurian cycle Idylls of the King?
questions.x: Tennyson worked on the Idylls for about 40 years and became poet laureate in 1850. He also wrote In Memoriam.

questions.q: Which Scottish poet is credited with writing 'Auld Lang Syne'?
questions.x: Burns sent the song to a collector in 1788 and said he had taken it down from an old man's singing. It is traditionally sung at New Year.

questions.q: Which Irish poet won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Yeats was the first Irish writer to win the prize. He later served as a senator of the Irish Free State.

questions.q: Which Irish poet won the 1995 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.x: Heaney's collections include Death of a Naturalist. His poems often draw on rural life in Northern Ireland, where he grew up on a farm.

questions.q: Who wrote the semi-autobiographical novel The Bell Jar?
questions.x: It appeared in 1963 under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas, a month before Plath died. It was published under her own name in 1966.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1969 memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings?
questions.x: It is the first of seven autobiographies by Angelou, who read her poem at Bill Clinton's 1993 inauguration.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1952 novel Invisible Man?
questions.x: It won the 1953 National Book Award. Ellison's novel is not about a literal invisible person but about social invisibility.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek tragedian wrote Medea?
questions.x: The play was first staged in 431 BC. Euripides is known for giving his female characters strong psychological depth.

questions.q: Which Greek philosopher's Poetics discusses tragedy and the idea of catharsis?
questions.x: Aristotle argued that tragedy purges the audience's pity and fear. The Poetics is the earliest surviving work of dramatic theory.

questions.q: What is it called when a sentence runs over a line break in poetry without a pause?
questions.x: The word comes from the French for 'straddling.' A caesura, by contrast, is a pause within a line.

questions.q: Which fixed poetic form has 19 lines and two repeating refrains?
questions.x: Dylan Thomas's 'Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night' is the most famous English villanelle. Elizabeth Bishop's 'One Art' is another.

questions.q: Under what pen name did the young Charles Dickens publish his early newspaper sketches?
questions.x: Sketches by Boz appeared in 1836. Boz was a family nickname for Dickens's younger brother.

questions.q: Which Bronte sister wrote The Tenant of Wildfell Hall?
questions.x: Anne's 1848 novel features a woman who leaves her abusive husband. It was a bold subject for its time.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare tragedy is the shortest of the tragedies?
questions.x: Macbeth runs about 2,100 lines, roughly half the length of Hamlet. Hamlet is Shakespeare's longest play.

questions.q: How many plays were printed in Shakespeare's First Folio of 1623?
questions.x: Half of the 36 plays, including Macbeth and The Tempest, had never been printed before and might have been lost without the Folio.

questions.q: In which Shakespeare play does the stage direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear' appear?
questions.x: The direction occurs in Act 3 and is one of the most famous in drama. Scholars debate whether a real bear or an actor in a costume was used.

questions.q: In Twelfth Night, what name does Viola use when she disguises herself as a man?
questions.x: Viola's disguise creates a tangle of mistaken love. Her twin brother Sebastian, whom she thinks is dead, finally appears.

questions.q: Who is Hamlet's loyal friend who survives the play?
questions.x: Hamlet asks Horatio to tell his story to the world. Horatio is a fellow student from Wittenberg.

questions.q: At which Danish castle is Hamlet set?
questions.x: Elsinore is the English name for Helsingor. Kronborg Castle there is traditionally associated with the play.

questions.q: Which Jane Austen novel features Anne Elliot and Captain Wentworth?
questions.x: Persuasion was Austen's last completed novel and was published posthumously in 1817. Its heroine is 27, old by the standards of the time.

questions.q: Which Dickens novel centers on the endless lawsuit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce?
questions.x: Published in 1852-53, it mocks the slow Court of Chancery. The lawsuit is so old that no one remembers what it is about.

questions.q: In which Dickens novel does the falsely humble clerk Uriah Heep appear?
questions.x: Heep repeatedly insists that he is 'umble'. Dickens called David Copperfield his 'favourite child' among his novels.

questions.q: Which 1873 Mark Twain novel, co-written with Charles Dudley Warner, gave a name to an era?
questions.x: The satirical novel of greed and corruption lent its title to the late 19th-century period of American history.

questions.q: Which Henry David Thoreau book recounts his time living in a cabin by a pond in Massachusetts?
questions.x: Thoreau lived by Walden Pond from 1845 to 1847. The book compresses his two years into a single seasonal cycle.

questions.q: Which Upton Sinclair novel exposed conditions in the Chicago meatpacking industry?
questions.x: Published in 1906, it led to the Pure Food and Drug Act. Sinclair said he aimed for the public's heart but hit its stomach.

questions.q: What is the name of the fictional Alabama town in To Kill a Mockingbird?
questions.x: Harper Lee modeled Maycomb on her hometown of Monroeville, Alabama. Atticus Finch is a lawyer there.

questions.q: What is the name of Don Quixote's horse?
questions.x: Don Quixote gives the thin, old horse a grand name that means 'formerly a work horse'. Babieca was the horse of El Cid.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek playwright wrote Antigone?
questions.x: Sophocles wrote about 120 plays, but only seven survive complete. Antigone is one of his three Theban plays.

questions.q: Which Dostoevsky novel has Prince Myshkin as its hero?
questions.x: Dostoevsky intended to portray a truly good man in a corrupt society. The novel was published in 1868-69.

questions.q: Which Russian author wrote the novel Fathers and Sons?
questions.x: Published in 1862, it popularized the word 'nihilist' through its character Bazarov. It is a classic of the generational clash.

questions.q: Which Melville story features a clerk who repeatedly says 'I would prefer not to'?
questions.x: Bartleby gradually refuses all work, until he refuses to leave the office. The story is set on Wall Street and was published in 1853.

questions.q: Which moor is the setting for The Hound of the Baskervilles?
questions.x: Doyle's 1902 Sherlock Holmes novel is set in Devon. He heard the local legend of a spectral hound from a friend.

questions.q: From which French region does Dumas's hero d'Artagnan come?
questions.x: Gascons were famously proud and quick-tempered, which suits d'Artagnan. The real d'Artagnan was a captain of the king's musketeers.

questions.q: Which Jane Austen novel is set partly in Bath and parodies Gothic fiction?
questions.x: Austen wrote it around 1798-99, but it was published posthumously in 1817. Its heroine Catherine Morland loves reading Gothic romances.
